description: Color spaces and gamut/transfer functions decomposed. Video codecs operate on YCbCr (or YUV) but the chroma representation, bit depth, gamut primaries, and transfer function all vary by content type. SDR uses BT.709 primaries + BT.1886/sRGB gamma; HDR uses BT.2020 primaries + PQ (Perceptual Quantizer) or HLG (Hybrid Log-Gamma) transfer functions. The mapping between RGB and YCbCr is itself a linear transform — but the gamut and gamma choices affect compression efficiency and visual fidelity dramatically.

sub_mechanisms.name: rgb_to_ycbcr_transform
sub_mechanisms.definition: Linear matrix: Y = a*R + b*G + c*B; Cb = (B - Y) / d; Cr = (R - Y) / e. Coefficients (a,b,c,d,e) differ by standard: BT.601 (SDTV), BT.709 (HDTV), BT.2020 (UHDTV).
sub_mechanisms.why: Decorrelates luma (Y, ~luminance) from chroma (Cb, Cr, ~color difference). After this transform, the chroma channels are smaller in dynamic range and can be subsampled (4:2:0) without much perceptual loss. Compression efficiency improves substantially vs RGB.

sub_mechanisms.name: chroma_subsampling_4_2_0
sub_mechanisms.definition: 4:2:0: full luma resolution, chroma at 1/2 horizontal and 1/2 vertical (1/4 the samples). Each chroma sample represents a 2x2 luma block.
sub_mechanisms.why: HVS spatial resolution is ~3-4x higher for luma than chroma. Subsampling chroma saves 50% of total samples with imperceptible quality loss at typical viewing distance. Standard for VOD streaming, broadcast, and consumer video.

sub_mechanisms.name: chroma_subsampling_4_2_2
sub_mechanisms.definition: 4:2:2: full luma resolution, chroma at 1/2 horizontal but full vertical (1/2 the samples).
sub_mechanisms.why: Better than 4:2:0 for content with vertical color detail (chroma keying for video production). Used in broadcast contribution feeds + professional video.

sub_mechanisms.name: chroma_subsampling_4_4_4
sub_mechanisms.definition: 4:4:4: no chroma subsampling. Each pixel has full luma + chroma.
sub_mechanisms.why: Required for screen content (text/graphics with sharp chroma edges) and high-end production. Same compression efficiency hit as RGB but preserves all chroma detail.

sub_mechanisms.name: BT_709_primaries
sub_mechanisms.definition: HDTV color gamut: defined by primary chromaticities (Rxy, Gxy, Bxy) on the CIE 1931 chromaticity diagram. Smaller than BT.2020.
sub_mechanisms.why: Match the phosphor primaries of CRT-era television. Backward-compatible with most consumer displays. Still the default for SDR streaming. The narrower gamut requires less bit precision than BT.2020 to avoid banding.

sub_mechanisms.name: BT_2020_primaries
sub_mechanisms.definition: UHDTV color gamut: significantly wider primaries than BT.709 (closer to spectrum locus). Covers ~75% of CIE chromaticity vs BT.709's ~36%.
sub_mechanisms.why: Future-proofs for modern displays (laser projection, quantum-dot OLED) that can reproduce wider colors. Used by HDR content. Requires 10+ bits per channel to avoid banding in the larger gamut.

sub_mechanisms.name: BT_1886_transfer_function
sub_mechanisms.definition: SDR gamma: V_out = (V_in)^2.4. Maps linear light to display drive voltage.
sub_mechanisms.why: Matches CRT phosphor response. Allocates more bit precision to dark regions (where HVS sensitivity is higher) than bright regions. Standard for SDR delivery.

sub_mechanisms.name: PQ_perceptual_quantizer
sub_mechanisms.definition: HDR10's transfer function: maps absolute luminance (up to 10,000 nits) to 10-bit code values via a perceptual quantisation curve based on the HVS contrast sensitivity function.
sub_mechanisms.why: Allocates bit precision proportional to HVS sensitivity. Display-referred (absolute luminance, not relative). PQ's bit precision is consistent across the dynamic range, unlike BT.1886 which under-allocates highlights.

sub_mechanisms.name: HLG_hybrid_log_gamma
sub_mechanisms.definition: Alternative HDR transfer function: linear in dark regions (like SDR gamma), logarithmic in bright regions. Scene-referred (relative luminance).
sub_mechanisms.why: Backward-compatible with SDR displays: an HLG signal looks acceptable on SDR. Good for broadcast where both SDR and HDR receivers exist. Less precise than PQ at peak brightness; better SDR compatibility.

sub_mechanisms.name: bit_depth_8_10_12
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-channel bit depth: 8-bit (256 levels, SDR), 10-bit (1024 levels, HDR/UHD), 12-bit (4096 levels, high-end HDR/Dolby Vision).
sub_mechanisms.why: Higher bit depth avoids banding (visible quantisation steps) especially in smooth gradients. PQ's wider luminance range requires 10+ bits to maintain BT.1886's perceptual precision. Compression efficiency drops slightly at higher bit depths.

sub_mechanisms.name: wide_color_gamut
sub_mechanisms.definition: Display capability to reproduce colors beyond BT.709. Different gamuts: DCI-P3 (cinema), Display-P3 (Apple devices), Rec.2020 (UHDTV target).
sub_mechanisms.why: Each gamut defines a different addressable color volume. Content authored for one gamut requires conversion (potentially clipping) when shown on a different one. Per-display tone-mapping is the renderer's job.

sub_mechanisms.name: tone_mapping
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-frame or per-shot mapping from source HDR luminance to display capabilities. HDR10 uses static metadata (one curve for the whole stream); HDR10+/Dolby Vision use dynamic metadata (per-scene curves).
sub_mechanisms.why: Displays vary in peak brightness (200 nits for entry SDR, 1000+ for HDR TVs, 4000+ for reference monitors). Tone mapping squeezes the source's dynamic range into the display's capability. Done well, preserves apparent brightness; done poorly, loses highlights or crushes shadows.

derivation_rules.name: ycbcr_decorrelation_enables_chroma_subsampling
if: luma and chroma are linearly separated into independent channels
then: chroma can be subsampled with minimal perceptual loss
derivation_rules.why: Decorrelation moves the bulk of image information into luma; chroma carries residual color details. HVS spatial sensitivity is lower for chroma, so chroma can be subsampled. RGB doesn't have this property — all three channels carry equal information.

derivation_rules.name: bit_depth_must_scale_with_gamut
then: bit depth must increase to avoid banding
derivation_rules.why: Banding visibility depends on the perceptual step size between code values. Wider gamut means each code value represents a larger color step (same code precision spread over more color). 10-bit is the minimum for BT.2020 to maintain ~JND-level precision.

derivation_rules.name: pq_allocates_bits_to_hvs_sensitivity
if: bit precision is allocated by HVS sensitivity
then: banding is hidden across the full dynamic range
derivation_rules.why: PQ's curve is derived from the HVS contrast sensitivity function. Equal-spaced PQ code values represent equal-spaced perceptual brightness levels — exactly where banding would otherwise be visible. BT.1886's gamma curve mismatches HVS sensitivity at high luminances.

derivation_rules.name: hlg_compatibility_trades_precision_for_backward_play
if: a stream must look acceptable on SDR displays
then: HLG's hybrid curve provides backward compatibility at the cost of HDR precision
derivation_rules.why: HLG's linear-in-darks segment matches BT.1886; SDR displays see acceptable mid-tones. PQ is purely HDR (looks wrong on SDR). Trade-off depends on deployment context — streaming can choose, broadcast often needs HLG.

derivation_rules.name: dynamic_tone_mapping_preserves_perceptual_intent
then: dynamic tone-mapping metadata (HDR10+, Dolby Vision) preserves intent better than static
derivation_rules.why: Static metadata (HDR10) applies one tone curve across the stream — wrong for any single shot. Dynamic metadata gives the renderer per-shot guidance. Cost: extra metadata bits (~kbps); benefit: dramatically better SDR-display rendering of HDR content.
